name: pipeline
intent: Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own.
problem: A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.
context: Processing that naturally decomposes into successive transformations of the same payload - request handling, ETL, compiler passes, message enrichment, image or byte-stream processing - whether the payload is a single value or a stream. It fits in-process, staged execution where one driver owns ordering, error handling and cancellation; distributing the stages across processes, transports and independently deployed filters is the architectural pipe-and-filter pattern instead.
benefits: Every step gains a name and a single responsibility, and the order of the whole transformation is declared once and read top to bottom instead of being implied by statement sequence.
Stages become interchangeable parts: a stage can be inserted, replaced, reordered or shared between pipelines without editing the stages around it.
Testing and instrumentation get a seam per stage: a step can be exercised alone, and a failure or a latency spike can be attributed to a named stage rather than to "the transform".
Streaming realizations pass one item through all stages at a time, so intermediate collections are never materialised, memory stays bounded and short-circuiting stops upstream work early.

Because stages are independent per item, the driver or runtime can overlap them, turning the sequence into an assembly line whose throughput is no longer bound by one worker passing every item through every step.
Error, cancellation and observability policy is applied at one place (the driver and the stage contract) instead of being scattered through the transformation logic.
tradeoffs: Stage boundaries erase shared context: a stage sees only the previous stage's output, so cross-cutting data such as request id, user or deadline must travel inside the payload or in an ambient context, and a stage that needs two earlier values forces an artificial intermediate type.

Every hop is a call through the stage contract; boxed or erased payloads (Object, any, interface{}, std::function, dyn callables) block fusion and inlining, so one hand-written fused loop is usually faster for short transformations.

A sequential pipeline serialises latency per item: none of stage 2 runs before stage 1 finishes that item, and overlapping stages requires buffering or concurrency, which in turn requires backpressure, completion and ordering bookkeeping.

Error semantics are not compositional: a mid-pipeline failure leaves partial work, every stage must share an agreed policy (fail fast, collect, compensate) and upstream producers must be cancelled or drained, or blocked senders and orphaned resources remain.
Debugging gets harder than a plain call stack: stack traces and profilers show the driver's frames, so a stage must be instrumented explicitly if per-stage timing and failure attribution are wanted.

Order becomes a hidden contract: reordering two stages (sanitise before validate, authorise before business logic) can silently change results, and assembling stages from configuration moves that contract from compile time to run time.

participants.responsibility: Supplies the initial payload or stream and owns the resource being read; it is the only participant with no upstream stage.
One named transformation with a single responsibility: consumes the previous stage's output, produces the next stage's input, and owns only its own state and configuration.

The shared signature and type that let heterogeneous implementations (functions, adaptor closures, handler objects, generator functions, publishers) sit in the same pipeline; it fixes the payload shape and the failure/cancellation channel.
Holds the ordered sequence of stages and executes it (loop, channel wiring, operator chain, subscription), forwarding payloads and propagating errors, cancellation and completion.
Consumes the final output - a terminal operation, writer or subscriber - and in lazy realizations is what triggers the execution of the whole pipeline.
The agreed per-stage behaviour when a stage fails, times out or is cancelled, plus the instrumentation hooks (stage name in logs, timings, counters) the driver applies uniformly.

use_cases: Request handling: deserialise, authenticate, validate, enrich, persist and render a request, with each step named so a failing stage is attributable and testable in isolation.
ETL and data import: extract, clean, transform, validate and load large files as a stream, so no intermediate collection is materialised and memory stays bounded.

Compiler and interpreter passes: source, tokens, AST, resolution, optimisation and code emission, where each pass is an independent stage over the intermediate representation and the pass list is the pipeline.
Message enrichment in an integration flow: unwrap, translate, enrich and route a message, one stage per concern, with per-channel ordering; the cross-process version stays pipe-and-filter.
Image or byte-stream processing: decode, crop or resize, watermark and encode, lazily per frame or chunk, optionally overlapping stages across cores.
Configuration-driven data cleaning: the stage list is assembled from configuration or a plugin registry so different tenants get different ordered steps without changing the stages themselves.

TensorFlow tf.data input pipelines: tf.data.Dataset pipelines that chain map, prefetch, parallel_interleave and shuffle stages to feed a training loop efficiently, with each stage independently configurable and the whole pipeline testable in isolation.

LLM token streaming: HTTP server-sent event streams where an LLM produces tokens at inference speed while clients consume at variable network speed; stream.pipeline() prevents the inference server from buffering unbounded tokens in memory when a slow client disconnects (Node.js stream backpressure case study).

Observability telemetry pipelines: OpenTelemetry Collector chains receivers, processors (memory_limiter, batch, filter, transform, tail_sampling) and exporters for traces, metrics and logs, with connectors (e.g., spanmetrics) bridging signal types and memory_limiter placed first to prevent OOM before filtering.

Typed TypeScript pipeline with schema validation: Zod or io-ts schemas define the stage contract at each boundary, catching schema violations at the exact stage that produced bad data rather than at a distant consumer.

Async generator pipelines in Python: asyncio queues with bounded capacity connect async generator stages, propagating backpressure by pausing producers when the queue is full; the FinStream analytics case study showed 82% memory reduction and 99.7% latency reduction versus unbounded buffering.

Event-streaming pipelines with Kafka and Flink: producers, topic partitions, Flink consumers and checkpointing form a distributed pipeline where backpressure cascades across every boundary; the Kafka max.block.ms and Flink backpressure.sample.interval settings interact under partition saturation and must be tested together under load.

Dynamic pipeline parallelism: construct-and-run pipelines (MapReduce, Spark) fix stage count at construction, while on-the-fly pipelines (Cilk-P Piper algorithm) allow the structure to emerge at runtime, varying per iteration and supporting data-dependent branching; on-the-fly enables pipelines like x264 that cannot be expressed with a fixed static structure.

LLVM compiler pass pipelines: PassBuilder assembles ModulePassManager, CGSCCPassManager, FunctionPassManager and LoopPassManager across the IR hierarchy (Module → CGSCC → Function → Loop), with registered callbacks injecting passes at named extension points (pipeline-start, vectorizer-start, optimizer-last); incorrect PreservedAnalyses declarations invalidate all downstream analyses.

Continuous data pipelines at scale (Google model): periodic pipelines run on cron and suffer from depth growth and resource exhaustion as organic load increases; continuous pipelines (master-slave or event-triggered) replace idle-waiting with always-on processing, eliminating the 'pipeline vs cron' discontinuity at the cost of operational complexity.

ML pipeline orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster): each orchestrator applies the pipeline pattern at the workflow level - Airflow's DAG-of-tasks, Kubeflow's per-container-step pipelines with GPU scheduling, Prefect's monoflow/subflow/orchestrator pattern, and Dagster's software-defined assets where asset dependencies imply the pipeline; the pipeline is the scheduler's unit of execution, not an implementation detail.
Apache Beam: PCollections flow through composable PTransforms (ParDo, Combine and GroupByKey) in a pipeline graph, making each transform boundary explicit while the runner handles execution.

Node.js stream.pipeline(): Readable, Transform and Writable stages compose with built-in backpressure, error propagation and AbortSignal cancellation; this is a concrete streaming realization, not a durable workflow engine.
avoid_when: Two or three fixed calls in one place: sequential calls with named intermediate variables are clearer than a stage list plus a driver.
Steps must branch, loop or run conditionally per item: a pipeline is a linear sequence, so use explicit control flow or a workflow/process manager.
A handler may decline to handle and pass control along without producing a result: chain-of-responsibility models that negotiation, a pipeline does not - every stage runs and produces the next input.
Stages are independent filters connected across processes, threads or transports with their own routing: use pipe-and-filter, the architectural counterpart, rather than a local pipeline.
The transformation is a single pure value transformation with no staging, reuse or per-stage policy: a composed function (function-composition) suffices.
The order is not known at assembly time, or individual stages must be retried or resumed over hours: a durable workflow engine is a better fit than an in-memory pipeline.
anti_patterns: God stage: one "process" stage that hides four steps, so the pipeline adds names without decomposing anything.
Pipeline of trivial stages: wrapping every one-liner in a stage object, adding indirection and per-stage overhead with no seam anyone uses.
Hidden state in stages: stages that mutate shared objects or module state make the result depend on execution order and history, so reordering or re-running silently changes behaviour.
Pipeline as an if-chain: stages that each inspect a flag and skip themselves - conditional logic wearing a pipeline costume, with the branching scattered instead of visible.
Silent error swallowing: stages that catch and drop failures to keep the chain going, so the pipeline reports success over corrupted data.
Rebuilding the pipeline per call: assembling stage lists, closures or subscriptions on the hot path instead of once at initialisation, paying allocation and dispatch on every item.

Unbounded buffers between stages: any queue, channel or buffer with no capacity limit between a producer and consumer eventually exhausts memory — Python asyncio.Queue(maxsize=0), Node.js without highWaterMark, or a Kafka consumer without lag limits are the common forms; the fix is always to bound the buffer and decide what to do when it is full.

Ignoring write() or push() return values: the most common production streaming bug in Node.js and RxJava; when a Writable's write() returns false or a Readable's push() returns false, the pipeline must pause — not calling drain or request() causes memory to grow until the process is OOM-killed (Node.js streams documentation, FlowVerify case study).

Consumer lag amplification in Kafka: the broker decouples producers from consumers, so slow downstream processing manifests as growing consumer lag rather than backpressure on the producer; without explicit lag alerts and max.poll.interval.ms tuning, a slow consumer silently accumulates an ever-larger replay backlog until retention expires (Wicked Smart Data backpressure case study).

GC death spiral from buffering: a consumer that falls behind causes data to accumulate in buffers, which increases GC pressure, which makes the consumer slower still, which causes more accumulation — the fix is to bound the buffer and shed load or slow the producer, not to add memory (Wicked Smart Data, ADHDecode backpressure analysis).

Broken backpressure chain in custom Transform: a Node.js Transform that calls its callback immediately without waiting for the downstream writable to drain breaks the pause/resume cycle at that stage, causing the upstream to continue filling memory while the Transform appears stalled — the fix is to await the drain event before invoking the callback.

Using pipe() instead of pipeline() in Node.js: pipe() does not destroy source streams when a downstream stream errors, leaving file descriptors and memory resident until process exit; pipeline() from stream/promises calls destroy() on every participant automatically.

Async generator unbounded buffering in Python: naive async generators yield items faster than consumers process them, queueing everything in memory with no natural throttling — the symptom is linear memory growth with item count; the fix is an explicit bounded asyncio.Queue with a semaphore or adaptive batch sizing.

Kafka-Flink version mismatch under partition saturation: Kafka 4.0 changed max.block.ms default from 30s to 60s and Flink 2.0 reduced backpressure.sample.interval from 1000ms to 100ms; together under partition saturation they created a cascading stall with 89% producer timeout rate and checkpoint stalls — the pair must be integration-tested under load before upgrading (johal.in postmortem).

Hot Observable and reactive pull backpressure: hot Observables (mouse events, stock prices, PublishProcessor) emit regardless of subscriber demand, so reactive pull backpressure does not apply; using request() on a hot source silently has no effect; must use onBackpressureBuffer/Drop/Latest or throttle operators instead.

Compiler pass PreservedAnalyses omission: a transformation pass that does not declare PreservedAnalyses correctly invalidates all downstream analyses, forcing the pass manager to recompute them from scratch and adding compile-time overhead proportional to the number of invalidated passes.

Dead-letter queue omission in streaming producers: producers without a DLQ for failed events permanently lose data when backpressure causes retries to exhaust — a 1.2M event loss in a Kafka/Flink recommendation pipeline was fully recovered post-outage by adding a DLQ topic and a nightly retry job.

Unbounded sending_queue in OTel Collector exporters: a sending_queue with queue_size unlimited by default grows until memory is exhausted when the backend is unreachable; set queue_size explicitly and configure max_elapsed_time for retry to prevent indefinite retry loops.
design_principles: Single responsibility: each stage performs exactly one transformation at one level of abstraction, which is what makes it replaceable.
Open/closed: behaviour is extended by inserting or substituting a stage, not by editing the driver or the neighbouring stages.
Composition over inheritance: the pipeline is an ordered assembly of collaborators, not a template-method hierarchy of subclasses.
Narrow contracts / least knowledge: a stage receives its input and its own configuration, not the whole pipeline or unrelated collaborators.
Fail fast at boundaries: the earlier a stage validates, the less work is discarded and the more local the failure stays.
Separation of concerns: transformation logic lives in the stages; ordering, error, cancellation and observability policy live in the driver.

Typed stage contracts at every boundary: schemas (Zod, io-ts, Protocol Buffers) catch contract violations at the producing stage rather than at a distant consumer; the stage name in the error message directly identifies the faulty step.
Backpressure is cooperative, not automatic: every stage must actively propagate the slow-consumer signal upstream; ignoring write() or request() return values silently disables the safety mechanism.
best_practices: Name every stage as a verb phrase and keep it to one responsibility; the stage names are the pipeline's documentation.
Define the stage contract once (payload type plus failure/cancellation channel) and keep it narrow; adapt existing functions at the edges instead of widening the contract.
Validate early and make the driver's failure behaviour explicit - abort, collect errors, retry or compensate - then test that behaviour, not only the happy path.
Instrument per stage (name, duration, item counts) because stack traces no longer show the chain.
Assemble the pipeline once at initialisation or per configuration, never per item, and keep stages stateless or explicitly state-scoped.
Test stages individually and the assembled order with order-sensitive cases, including the empty pipeline and the single-stage pipeline.
Keep the in-process version local and readable; when stages become independently deployable, switch to the pipe-and-filter architecture deliberately.

Bound every buffer between stages; a full buffer is a signal, not a failure. Use highWaterMark or equivalent to make the bound explicit — unbounded buffers are OOMs in slow motion (arc42 backpressure propagation).

Always use the framework's pipeline-composition primitive (stream.pipeline() in Node.js, tokio::mpsc bounded channels in Rust, Go buffered channels) over manual pipe() chains or fire-and-forget sends — the composed form propagates errors and backpressure correctly across every stage.

Respect backpressure signals at every stage: honor write() returning false, push() returning false, and Subscription.request(n) in Reactive Streams; ignoring them is the leading cause of streaming OOM in production (Node.js streams documentation, RxJava MissingBackpressureException analysis).

Test backpressure explicitly: set highWaterMark to a small value (e.g. 64 bytes), connect a consumer that deliberately pauses with a sleep, and verify that process.memoryUsage().heapUsed stays flat over 60 seconds — growing memory means backpressure is not propagating (Node.js stream backpressure guide).

Place memory_limiter first in OTel Collector and Kafka Streams processor chains to prevent OOM before any filtering or enrichment work is done; all downstream processors then operate on bounded memory.

Tune highWaterMark to workload: the 16 KB default is conservative for file/streaming workloads where 64–256 KB reduces per-chunk overhead; for object-mode streams use 16–100 objects depending on object size; wrong values hurt throughput.

For reactive streams: prefer Flux/Flowable over Observable when backpressure is needed; distinguish hot sources (which cannot be backpressured) from cold sources (which respond to request()) and apply onBackpressureBuffer/Drop/Latest on hot sources.

In compiler pass pipelines: always declare PreservedAnalyses correctly in getAnalysisUsage(); missing declarations invalidate all downstream analyses, adding compile-time cost proportional to the analysis depth.

Separate pipeline orchestrator (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster) from experiment tracker (MLflow, W&B) from feature store; making one tool do all three creates a tangle; each stage of the ML pipeline maps to one DAG node or asset, not to an entire platform.

Add dead-letter queues (DLQ) for streaming stages: set retry count (3–5), configure a DLQ topic for exhausted events, and run a nightly job to reprocess DLQ backlog with alerting when events age past 24 hours.

Use the adaptive backpressure strategy for async generator pipelines: start with buffer_size = (producer_rate − consumer_rate) × acceptable_delay; monitor buffer growth rate and consumer lag in addition to buffer size — a stable buffer with rising lag indicates an upstream problem.

Monitor OTel Collector pipelines with standing alerts on otelcol_processor_refused_spans, otelcol_processor_dropped_spans, otelcol_exporter_send_failed_spans and exporter queue_size approaching capacity; these are the leading indicators of backpressure before latency spikes appear.
